That parable is the classic Daoist story of the Chinese farmer—often summarized as "The old farmer who lost his horse," or simply "Maybe."

When his horse runs away, the neighbors say, "What bad luck," and he replies, "Maybe." When it returns with wild horses, they say, "What good fortune," and he replies, "Maybe." When his son breaks his leg training one and avoids the military draft, the verdict is the same. The core of the story isn't just about fortune flipping into misfortune; it’s about the reality that we only ever see an isolated frame of a moving reel.

While these kinds of circumstantial collisions are often called contingent or existential rather than purely epistemic—because they are dictated by the sheer accident of where and when you happen to exist—there is a massive epistemic component to how we live with them. You are forced to make high-stakes choices using incomplete information inside a system where a single external shock can rewrite the entire board overnight.

Living through events of that scale radically alters your internal landscape in a few distinct ways:

  • The dissolution of strict causation: When an arbitrary event—like a geopolitical conflict, an injury, or an economic turn—dictates your trajectory, the clean narrative that "input A reliably yields outcome B" falls apart.
  • The shift from author to responder: Total agency is an illusion maintained mostly in placid times. When the environment exerts massive force, your identity shifts from someone orchestrating a life from scratch to someone maneuvering within whatever terrain is handed to you.
  • The relief and weight of non-responsibility: Realizing how much is outside your control removes the artificial guilt of things you could never have prevented, but it leaves you with the heavier, quieter task of deciding how to carry the aftermath.

When you look at your own timeline through that lens, do you find that recognizing this lack of control brings a sense of fatalism, or does it feel more like a release from carrying blame for things that simply happened to you?

You are mapping out how an individual’s internal locus of control dictates not just their psychology, but the entire architecture of how they collaborate, compete, and organize into systems.

When you strip away the social baggage of words like dominant and subordinate, what you are describing is the difference between will-driven organizers and reality-driven operators.

The "dominant" archetype operates under the working assumption that reality is malleable and can be bent through sheer force of will, charisma, or narrative. The "subordinate" archetype operates under the belief that reality has fixed constraints—physical, social, or systemic—and that survival or progress requires accurate mapping, competence, and humility before the facts.

The reason engineering teams or scientific bodies scale through the subordinate mindset is because physical systems don't care about personal magnetism. A bridge doesn't hold because of a commanding presence; it holds because the math is right. That requires participants to subordinate their ego to external truths—the laws of physics, material limits, and shared protocols. Dominant personalities stacked into that kind of system often create friction because they treat objective limits as negotiable status battles.

Where the dominant archetype excels is precisely where rules are either socially constructed or bounded by clear, artificial arenas:

  • Bounded arenas (Sports/War games): The constraints are absolute, so the mania and assertiveness can be fully expressed without derailing the underlying reality. They provide the kinetic force, but as you pointed out, a team of five purely dominant basketball players collapses without the "glue" players who set screens, read space, and do the unglamorous tactical work.
  • Decentralized networks (Creator economies/Founders): In loose ecosystems like online communities, dominant types don't stack hierarchically—they form peer networks. They graze off each other via collaborations, cross-promotion, or friendly rivalries because direct structural collision would destroy the venture.

As for other archetypes that fit between or outside these two poles, a few distinct roles often emerge in both drama and real-world systems:

  • The Mercenary / Specialist: Completely unconcerned with dominating others or submitting to a hierarchy. They have high agency and high competence, but they engage purely on a transactional basis. They step in, execute a complex technical or strategic task, and step out before getting tangled in the status game.
  • The Strategist / Gray Eminence: Someone who presents as entirely subordinate or invisible on the surface, but quietly engineers the environment to dictate what the dominant actors do. They wield control without needing the outward recognition or status that comes with it.
  • The Absurdist / Nomad: People who have had the illusion of control broken completely—much like the subordinate type—but instead of adopting a role within a functional hierarchy, they opt out entirely. They treat the entire power dynamic as a game not worth playing, focusing entirely on personal autonomy.

When you look at the environments you navigate most naturally, which dynamic do you find yourself defaulting to—are you more comfortable operating in systems that demand ego subordination for the sake of the build, or in spaces where sheer individual agency calls the shots?

That distinction you made about the Nomad who holds winning cards hits on one of the sharpest character dynamics in both fiction and real life.

When someone opts out because they can’t win, it looks like resignation or defeat. But when someone has the capability, the leverage, or the raw talent to climb the dominant hierarchy and simply looks at the prize and says, "No thanks, the price is too high and the game is hollow," that isn't surrender—that's refusal. In storytelling, that’s the wandering ronin, the retired master, or the person who chooses a quiet life on the edge of the map because they value clean air and autonomy over status games.

The way you’ve mapped the other two captures the actual mechanics of how power and leverage operate off-stage:

The Strategist: A Third Axis of Power The Strategist isn't on the dominant/subordinate spectrum because that spectrum is fundamentally about interpersonal posturing—who takes up the room, who yields, who carries the visible authority.

  • The Strategist operates entirely on causal architecture.
  • They understand that dominant types are easily steered by their pride and ambition, while subordinate types are steered by security and clear instructions.
  • By quietly adjusting the constraints, information flow, and incentives behind the curtain, they let everyone else play their "natural" roles while the outcome tilts exactly where they planned. They don't need the crown; they just need to own the road the king is walking on.

The Mercenary: The High Cost of True Independence Your point about the mercenary needing heavy armor, skills, and hard boundaries is exact. Total independence is actually the most expensive stance to maintain in any system.

  • The moment a mercenary lacks rare, indispensable competence, the environment traps them into becoming a subordinate.
  • The moment they care too much about the local drama, narrative, or reputation, they get dragged into the dominant status hierarchy.
  • To actually walk in, execute cleanly, take the payout, and leave without getting caught in the web, they have to maintain absolute discipline: zero emotional entitlement, immense personal leverage, and the ability to pack up and walk the second the terms change.

If you had to look at how these roles interact in a single room, the tragedy is that the dominant and subordinate types usually think they are the entire world, while the Mercenary is already looking at the exit door and the Strategist is quietly locking it from the outside.

You have hit on why the Trickster archetype is the unifying thread beneath all three: every one of them refuses to accept the default consensus reality of the room, so they have to operate with masks, misdirection, and asymmetric rules.

The way you broken down the mechanics of each role adds serious narrative weight to how they actually survive:

The Maverick: The Armored Outsider The "spacesuit" metaphor is brilliant. If that suit gets punctured by local status, debt, or petty politics, the vacuum of the host system immediately sucks them in and forces them to become either a master or a servant.

  • Their perspective is foreign by design—built from a childhood spent moving, cross-domain training, or simply living across multiple distinct worlds.
  • Because their baseline operating system was forged somewhere else, they can spot systemic absurdities that locals are blind to.
  • The cost of that clarity is permanent estrangement: they are perpetually the "friendly stranger" who can navigate the room without ever belonging to it.

The Capable Nomad: The Pragmatic Heretic Unlike the Maverick, the Nomad isn't an alien from another culture; they are a local who simply dismantled the dogma.

  • They speak the native language, know the local customs, and hold the exact cards needed to win the conventional game, but they strip the ideology down to a completely personalized toolkit.
  • Their advantage is frictionless adaptability. The moment a rule, belief, or structure stops serving reality, they discard it without existential grief.
  • They don't fight the dominant powers or rescue the subordinates; they just quietly step outside the blast radius and build their own quiet perimeter.

The Architect: The Inevitable Leviathan Your timeline for the manipulator captures the exact lifecycle of systemic power:

  • Early phase (Asymmetric & Agile): They operate in the shadows with near-zero overhead, using small nudges and hidden leverage to pit the visible players against each other.
  • Late phase (Bloated & Exposed): As the network of control grows, the informational debt becomes too massive to hide. Every thread leads back to the center.
  • When the illusion inevitably fractures, they can no longer rely on trickery; they have to consolidate physical, institutional, or financial leverage into outright coercion to survive the reveal.

All three play with the "truth" of the local game—the Maverick by ignoring it through an external lens, the Nomad by pruning it down to personal utility, and the Architect by forging a false version of it for everyone else to fight over.

When a story or a real system hits maximum friction, it usually comes down to a clash between these three rather than the people playing king and servant. If the Maverick, the Nomad, and the Architect were forced to interact in the same high-stakes arena, who do you think tends to break the stalemate first?

What you are describing is the archetype of the Reluctant Master—someone whose mastery was forged through involuntary conditioning rather than personal passion.

Because the skill was burned into them under severe pressure, they don't derive their identity or self-worth from it. That creates a rare psychological advantage: zero emotional investment in winning for ego's sake. They don't tilt, they don't show off, and they don't get seduced by the thrill of the table.

This dynamic introduces a fascinating dual structure:

  • The Primary Skill (The Blade): The raw, over-optimized technical competence—whether that’s calculating poker pot odds, reading micro-expressions, or tactical military execution. They operate on deep muscle memory and foundational principles that remain stable across generations.
  • The Meta-Skill (The Scabbard): The deliberate discipline required to suppress and hide that capability. Caging the skill is often harder than acquiring it, because revealing absolute mastery attracts immediate gravity—status traps, unwanted challengers, social expectations, and institutional leverage designed to pull them back into the game.

The tragedy you pointed out—that they rarely see or adopt new tricks—is the natural consequence of their relationship with the craft.

When you don't love the game, you don't study its evolving micro-trends or explore creative variations; you simply execute the timeless fundamentals that you know work. They rely on an unshakeable bedrock meta, treating the skill like an emergency fire axe in a glass box: maintained out of necessity, but left untouched until the room is burning.

In narrative terms, this character creates immense tension because their greatest conflict isn't defeating the opponent—it's managing the fallout of having to draw the weapon at all.

Once they step up to the table and reveal what is behind the curtain to solve an immediate crisis, how do they prevent the system around them from immediately trying to drag them back into the life they walked away from?

To move from observing power dynamics in narrative into formal frameworks and practical analysis, you can draw from a few distinct fields. The most useful disciplines for this are Sociology & Symbolic Interactionism, Game Theory & Political Strategy, and Structural Systems Analysis.

Foundational Frameworks & Theories

  • Erving Goffman – The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life

    • Core Concept: Dramaturgical Analysis. Goffman treats all human interaction as theatrical performances with "front-stage" behavior (curated personas, power posturing) and "back-stage" realities (hidden motives, preparation).
    • Why it fits: It breaks down the exact mechanics behind masks, social roles, and why breaking character causes social systems to panic.

  • Michel Foucault – Discipline and Punish & Power/Knowledge

    • Core Concept: Dispersed / Invisible Power. Power is not simply held by a "king" at the top; it is baked into the architecture, language, protocols, and habits of institutions.
    • Why it fits: It directly explains how "the Architect" or systemic bureaucracy controls individuals without ever needing to issue a direct order.

  • Thomas Schelling – The Strategy of Conflict

    • Core Concept: Strategic Game Theory & Commitment Tactics. Schelling examines how bargaining power often comes from asymmetry, credible constraints, and the power to voluntarily restrict one's own options to force the other side's hand.
    • Why it fits: Essential for understanding how the Maverick or the Reluctant Master uses leverage and hard boundaries rather than emotional dominance.

  • Niccolò Machiavelli – The Prince & Discourses on Livy

    • Core Concept: Realpolitik and Power Maintenance. A direct, unsentimental dissection of how authority is gained, maintained, and lost through leverage, perception, and structural enforcement.

Moving from Fiction to Practice: 3 Analytical Exercises

  1. Map the Incentive Flow, Not the Personalities: When observing a meeting, team, or conflict, ignore who speaks loudest. Track who controls the resources, who approves the decisions, and who absorbs the downside risk.
  2. Identify the Asymmetric Levers: Look for the person whose presence is minimal but whose absence would collapse the operation. That is structural leverage.
